The short version

Spotify keeps adding listeners and payers: 788 million monthly users and 306 million subscribers after the third quarter of 2026. Profit per euro of sales slipped for a second quarter, and the company expects it to recover in the fourth. The stock now costs about 43 times its last year of earnings, above the 34 where we would set it aside.

Spotify gets paid by people who subscribe, and by companies that buy ads around the music and the talk. Subscribers are the large line. Advertising is the smaller line. The company reports in euros, and the charts are in euros.

The third quarter of 2026 added 11 million monthly users and 6 million subscribers, to 788 million and 306 million. Revenue was 4,969 million euros. Operating margin slipped a second quarter in a row, to 13.5%, and the company guides the fourth quarter back up.

Premium is the engine, and it is still growing. Advertising is a real line, and it is not the engine. Monthly users are still compounding. What looks mature is the price of a subscription: the euros per Premium user have sat in a narrow band for years. The annual chart starts in 2018 because that is the first year in the file.

Every full year from 2018 through 2023 was an operating loss except 2021, a small profit of 94 million euros. 2024 and 2025 were operating profits of 1,365 and 2,198 million euros, and free cash flow rose with them. Capital spending is small beside that cash. Those bars are negative because the print is cash spent.

The weekly multiple is the share price divided by the last four quarters of earnings per share. The new four quarters earn less than the old ones, because the year-ago quarter carried a gain on its exchangeable notes and a tax benefit, so the multiple rose to about 36× when that quarter dropped out, and then to about 43× as the share price rose. Free cash flow did not carry that gain: the last four quarters brought in 3,190 million euros, and the latest week's price is about 40 times that cash per share.

Risks

  • The business breaks if people stop paying to listen, or if the cost of the music takes the profit back. The lines to watch are Premium subscribers, monthly users, euros per Premium user, and operating income.
  • Advertising moves with the ad market. It is the smaller line.
  • A price increase that subscribers refuse shows up as slower Premium adds and a weaker euro-per-user line.
  • Cash can shrink again if content costs or spending rise. Free cash flow is that line.

Close competitors

  • Apple Music — a subscription that rides along with the phone, so it does not need this ad line.
  • YouTube Music — Google's music service, attached to a huge free audience.
  • Amazon Music — bundled with a shopping membership.
  • Deezer — a smaller paid music service, mostly in Europe, selling the same kind of subscription.
  • Tencent Music — the large paid music service in China, a market this company does not lead.

How many free listeners become subscribers is written up separately. Premium divided by monthly users is the mix of the base, not that rate.

Open gaps

  1. Podcast hours and audiobook hours are blank in every period. There is no chart.
  2. Free-to-paid conversion is not disclosed. Premium divided by monthly users is the mix of the base, not that rate, and it is not drawn as conversion.
  3. A blended forward year was not printed, so that mark is blank. The latest official forward multiples are from 2026 week 44, using analyst estimates from 5 November 2026, after the third-quarter print: 48.0× on fiscal 2026 and 37.4× on fiscal 2027. Weeks 41 through 43 are the history marks for those weeks. Week 45 has a trailing mark and no official forward print yet.
  4. Revenue CAGR 15.5% for FY2021–FY2025 is already on the annual income chart, labeled derived. Gross profit CAGR 20.7%, operating income CAGR 119.9%, free cash flow CAGR 79.5%, and operating cash flow CAGR 68.8% are already on their charts for that same window, labeled derived. Net income has no CAGR on that window because 2021 net income is negative, so the ends are not both positive. Capital expenditure has no CAGR because the printed figures are negative cash outflows. Eight annual years are on the page.
  5. Year-over-year is blank for 2018 and its quarters because 2017 is not in the file. It is blank for the third quarter of 2020 and the second quarter of 2021, because the third quarter of 2019 and the second quarter of 2020 are not in the file. Ad-supported users were not printed in the fourth quarter of 2021, so that bar is blank and the year-over-year on that line is blank in the fourth quarter of 2022. Operating cash flow was not printed in the fourth quarter of 2021, so that bar is blank and its year-over-year is blank in the fourth quarter of 2022. Net adds are blank in the first quarter of 2018 because the fourth quarter of 2017 is not in the file. None of these is a prior of zero. A percent was not filled in.
  6. The third quarter of 2018, the third quarter of 2019, and the second quarter of 2020 are not in the file. They sit on every quarterly chart as blanks. Annual figures are the full-year print. They are not the sum of the quarters drawn beside them.
  7. Annual history starts in 2018. The weekly multiple starts at 2022 week 13 and runs through 2026 week 45, and the chart opens on the last six months. Earlier periods were not invented. Weeks with negative trailing earnings are blank, and the line does not connect across a blank. 2024 week 26 is blank: its Friday came before the June quarter closed, so it still uses the four quarters to March 2024, which sum to a net loss.
  8. The multiple is a dollar share price divided by euro earnings, not converted into one currency. The weekly price is the volume-weighted average of daily closes. Earnings switch to a new quarter in the first week whose Friday falls on or after the quarter's end, so weeks 40 through 45 of 2026 use the four quarters to September 2026, at 34.4× in week 40 and 43.0× in week 45. The same Friday rule now binds the December quarter in weeks 1–13 of 2025 and of 2026; the prior page had stayed on the September earnings until week 14.
  9. 2026 is not a full year. Nothing after the third quarter of 2026 is in the file. The fourth-quarter guide is the company's forecast and is not drawn as a result.
  10. Gross, operating, and net margins are income divided by revenue, labeled derived. Year-over-year is not drawn on that chart because those rates are not printed levels.
  11. From 2026 the company moves some revenue from advertising into Premium. The third and fourth quarters of 2025 are drawn as the company restated them on the new basis, so third-quarter 2026 growth matches the filing: Premium up 17%, advertising up 10%. Earlier quarters are as first printed. So the year-over-year points for the third and fourth quarters of 2025 are blank: each would set a restated quarter against the first print a year earlier. The first- and second-quarter 2026 growth rates still compare the new basis with the old one.
  12. Free cash flow over the last four quarters is the sum of four printed quarters, labeled derived. It is blank until four printed quarters are in the file, so it starts in the second quarter of 2021; the missing third quarters of 2018 and 2019 and second quarter of 2020 each blank the four sums that would include them.
  13. Price to free cash flow is the weekly dollar price over euro free cash flow per share for the last four quarters, with no currency conversion, labeled derived. It uses the same weeks, the same quarter switch, and the same diluted share count as the trailing multiple. It would be blank in any week where four-quarter free cash flow is zero or below; none of the drawn weeks is.
  14. Known chart limits, left as they are for now: the operating margin end label rounds 13.5% to 14%; the gate lines at 30× and 34× are solid, not dashed; the latest trailing value is labeled in copper, not the trailing line's colour; and some legends add "(hero)" to the highlighted series.
